utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters. I can see that they're all here. We can see better in this courtroom whether they are or not. [In English] Madam Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-33-T, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we haven't worked for some time, Mr. Harmon, would you introduce the Prosecution for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; good morning to my colleagues for the Defence. Today assisting me are my colleagues and co-counsel, Mr. Andrew Cayley to my right, and to his right, Mr. Peter McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Petrusic, would you present yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning to my colleagues of the Prosecution. The Defence is as it has been so far, myself, Mr. Petrusic, and my colleague on my left, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you too, General Krstic. We're going to take up the case where we left off. What do we have today, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, we have a protected witness, and in order to proceed with him we will need to lower the blinds. We anticipate calling today two, possibly three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We're going to have the blinds drawn for the moment and we'll raise them later on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Witness U.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness U. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you feel comfortable and are you rested? Perhaps you could draw your chair closer to the microphone, please, if you would. Witness U, we're going to refer to you in that way for reasons of security. You shall now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon is to your right. Your witness, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness U.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise to both you and Mr. Harmon, but we need the list with the witness' name for the Defence and for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic, for drawing our attention to that. I was thinking of that very same thing. Witness, I apologise, but before we begin, you're going to be shown a piece of paper with your name written on it. You will give us a yes or no answer whether it is your name or not. Just that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is, indeed, my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you. We are ready, I think. Mr. Harmon, I apologise for forgetting that, but I'm sure you had it in mind, and I should like to thank Mr. Petrusic for drawing it to our attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, could you tell us your nationality, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And are you from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I graduated from several secondary schools. My basic education was at the gymnasium, the general secondary school. I was not able to get a job straight away, so that I worked as an electrician for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, we're going to spend a lot of time today talking about radios, and you have told me about your interest in radios and I would appreciate it if you would tell the Judges when you became interested in radios and what types of special classifications or certificates you received in the pursuit of your interest in radios.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Your Honours, my interest started when I was 14. I was interested in electronics and radios, radio devices, which is when I attended a constructor's sector in the field, and graduated from that, and went on to a second course three years later. And I held a "C" classification in amateur radio, a radio ham. And do you wish me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Witness U, could you explain to the Judges what a "C" classification is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: A "C" classification for a radio ham is an examination which everybody passes in that field in the world. It is an international examination. It is composed of abbreviations for certain names, countries, and even sentences. You have to know calligraphy and work with radio devices, radios themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, in 1992 you joined the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you remained in active service in the JNA for 14 months; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have a speciality while you were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. I was a radio calligraphist, which included a teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the course of your service in the JNA, did you become familiar with the types of radio devices within your unit that were being used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In short, all the devices that my unit had in its possession and on the basis of textbooks, I was able to expand my knowledge considerably in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you left the JNA, Witness U, did you continue in the reserves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I did, from 1984 onwards, when I attended a seminar, a course, and got a rank. And I did the "B" category exam and was interested in radio -- became even more interested in radio electronics and radio devices, and I got the rank of sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Witness U, while you were in the JNA reserves, you continued to be involved with radios and radio communications; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to that, you pursued your interest in amateur radio and achieved what's called the "B" certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, Witness U, what is a "B" certificate in amateur radio; what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: A "B" certificate in radio amateurism is a higher category which requires a better knowledge of amateur radio communication, the handling of equipment, and more telegraphic signs, and you have to be more adapt in all fields and have to have a good knowledge of electronics as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, did you maintain your interest in radios and radio communication up until the time the conflict in Bosnia started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I even had my own radio transmitters, and I worked with different frequencies and bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you construct radio stations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Since 1982 or 1983, that was when I began constructing radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, I would now like to direct your attention to the time when the war started in Bosnia. Tell the Judges what you first did when the war started in order to serve your country.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, I worked for the civilian authorities and I was in a reserve formation. I assisted them in technical matters, in installations. I helped them install devices, develop radio networks, and installations, as I say, the installation and function. We use the term "visual reconnaissance stations"; that is the term we use. And also let me add -- just one moment, please, if I may take a minute. I worked with codes and plans for radio devices, drawing up plans for the functioning of radio devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you initially work in civil defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time, did you stop working for the civil defence authorities and start working for the army or for the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. On the (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And very, very generally, what were your duties and obligations when you made a transition from the civil defence authorities to the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you define the term "anti-electronic combat"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Anti-electronic combat consists of the following: It consists of monitoring and emission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Monitoring," by that do you mean monitoring the enemy communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what it does, and "emission" also means interception of those same facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you remain in the field of anti-electronic warfare until the conclusion of the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, until I was relieved of the services on the (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you just some general questions, Witness U. In the military, can you tell us very briefly, what's the purpose of intercepting enemy communications? Why do you do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: This is done so that we can detect on time the enemy movements, whether the enemy is advancing, whether they are encountering any problems, and to discover the intent, the enemy's intent, which are usually secret, confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, to your knowledge, did each of the parties in the war, the Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Serbs, the Croatian army, the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did each of those parties to the combat have an anti-electronic warfare unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this type of unit in which you served was a unit that was in all of the armies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the course of attempting to intercept and listen to communications of the enemy, do you also intercept communications that are encrypted, that are coded, and that are open-line communications with no encryption and no codes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Both, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to focus, Witness U, and I'd like you to give us very briefly, in very elementary terms, a lesson on how radios work, how communications work, and essentially how you intercept the communication. If you could first of all describe how radio communications are made and what you look for in terms of intercepting such a communication.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Radio communication is communication between two parties which is not a physical communication. It goes on the air, through the airwaves. For example, a radio communication can be established in the following way: You need two receivers and two transmitters which can work in a duplex fashion, which means that they are switched on all the time or partially. It functions in such a way that one of the participants has their transmitter and an antenna, and it emits its bands or wavelengths in code or encryption towards the receiver who also has an antenna for reception. That is how communication between the two parties is established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. We intercept this communication by positioning ourselves in a particular locality on one waveband. It is a selected location where communication already exists. We direct our antenna in the direction that we wish to have them function and then we usually wait. There is a waiting period until communication begins. Those are the initial steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Witness U, thank you for that brief lesson. Let me now focus your attention to the period in July of 1995 when the Srebrenica enclave fell to the Bosnian Serb army. First of all, can you tell the Judges the name of the unit in which you were serving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It was the Anti-Electronic Combat Company within the 2nd Corps, and I was in the (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to need the assistance of the usher because there's a map over here I'd like to show the witness, and it's ill-positioned if we intend to keep his identity protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let the usher hold next to you, Witness U, a Prosecutor's Exhibit which is a map. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 138. I don't know if it can be seen on the monitor in that position. Witness U, could you please point out to the Judges the specific location where the (redacted) of the Anti-Electronic Warfare Company was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: This is that locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to see where he's pointed in the circumstances, so perhaps instead of that, Mr. Usher, we could put an A3-sized --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, have you got something that we could place on the ELMO, perhaps, a document for the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think that's the easier way to proceed. Thank you. Mr. Usher, if you could move that up a bit, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, could you use the pointer, please, and point to the location where you and your unit was stationed at the time of the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I apologise, but it was not my platoon -- the question referred to my platoon, I thought. Was that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you, Witness U, is can you tell us where you and your men who were intercepting these radio communications were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I see. Yes, I can. This was the location where we intercepted communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has placed his pointer on a green dot that is identified as Okresanica. Thank you very much, Witness U. Mr. Usher, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, at Okresanica, were there other units beside your own unit engaged in monitoring enemy communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, there were other units too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you identify those units, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian authorities, the police, the 21st Brigade -- no, I'm sorry, the 21st Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So there were two units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Well, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I should say two beside your own unit. One of those units was the 21st Division of the Anti-Electronic Warfare Group, and I take it the other was a unit of the police. Was that a unit of the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's focus on your unit, (redacted). Witness U, how many men were in the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't get a translation for the last portion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, you said something that wasn't picked up by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And tell the Judges how you worked; what kind of shifts, how many people worked on a shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We had three shifts, one of which was the night shift. And depending on the activities, on the radio equipment, there were one to four men per shift. At night, there was one man and, if necessary, more, for reasons of economising with manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could, without placing on the ELMO, show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 300, which will be an exhibit that will be under seal. 300 is a list of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, this is not going to be made a public exhibit. I'm going to ask you: Did you assist me in preparing this exhibit, and did you identify the names of the individuals who served in your group of people intercepting radio communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I gave you the names in this order on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this list represents the people who were serving in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, without doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If that exhibit could be placed under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your position, Witness U, in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, how long had the platoon been stationed at Okresanica, intercepting enemy communications, prior to July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Almost two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, from the position of Okresanica, whose communications were you monitoring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We were able, from our position at Okresanica, to monitor the area of responsibility between three rivers, the Bosna, the Sava, and the Drina, in very general terms. Those are the three rivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you monitoring the communications of the HVO or were you monitoring the communications of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We were monitoring the communications of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the area that you've described to us, Witness U, is quite a large area in Bosnia, and I'd like to show you now Prosecutor's Exhibit 139, which is a map, and if this could be placed on the ELMO. Now, Witness U, this is a map that you've seen in my office before coming in to testify; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this map represents only a small area -- a small part of the area that was in your area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges what this particular exhibit represents? You can use the pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The map shows a part of the area of responsibility that we were covering. It is territory where the command centre was of the army of Republika Srpska, actually the central communications -- the communications centre that they had, radio relay centre, from where all radio relay communications were transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you point that out, please, on the ELMO, that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Of course. This is the radio relay centre marked here with the word "Panorama".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has pointed to the centre of an area from which a number of lines radiate out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, you said "Panorama". What is "Panorama"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: "Panorama" was the name of that radio centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that a code name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where is the radio relay centre located, near what town or in what town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The radio relay centre was in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was Han Pijesak the command centre for the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It was the main headquarters. The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Witness U, I'm sorry to have interrupted you. Could you continue on with your explanation of the various features identified on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The radio relay centre has several radio relay communications, as can be seen on the map. So this is the main participant. The central participant is linked with subordinate units. Here on the map we can see that there are at least two types of radio relay links, and there are several. Here we can see, for instance, how communication was established with individual brigades and corps, such as, for instance, you can see here the Bratunac Brigade, then the advanced command post of the Drina Corps, the former command post of the Drina Corps. We can also see here that the same radio relay transmission was not used. Then we have a link with Zlotrg, then the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, then Palma, which you can't see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you lower the exhibit so the Judges can see Palma.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "Palma", Witness U, again is Palma a code sign? If it is, with what unit is it associated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is the code name for the Zvornik Brigade, which we can see here now. All radio relay equipment was mounted on very high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your description, Witness U, you described Badem and you pointed out to the Judges the location of the Bratunac Brigade. Could you again point out for the Judges the radio communication line leading to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: From the radio relay centre towards the radio relay installations of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, is Badem the code name for the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when I say "code name" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We call it the secret name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, when one radio -- one person who wants to transmit a radio communication to the Bratunac Brigade, how would that transmitter -- how would the communicator refer to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: He would call them "Badem".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So he wouldn't identify the unit he was attempting to make communication with as the Bratunac Brigade; instead, he would identify that unit as Badem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me move the exhibit again to the left, and you have indicated the Drina Corps headquarters. Could you point that out on this map, and can you tell the Judges what their code name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. Their code name was Zlatar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, are there other code names that are identified on this map, code names for specific units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: There is Dora, Prostor, Gric, Vrelo, Matica, Bresa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, it's difficult to follow that. If you would merely take us on a tour of this map, point out the unit and the code name, where it is marked on this particular map, it would be helpful to us all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Bresa, the Sokolac Brigade, Matica, the Romanija Brigade; then we have Grmec in Skelani. That's as much as I can see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness U, to your left, can you see the large board that is to your left? It's Exhibit 137.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we use Prosecutor's Exhibit 137 and place that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, this is in English. Did you and I have an opportunity yesterday in my office to review this particular exhibit which identifies the code name of the VRS unit on the left and the corresponding unit on the right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this an accurate exhibit? Does it properly identify the code name with the corresponding unit on the right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, just to illustrate one more time, Witness U, if the Drina Corps headquarters, which was Zlatar, wanted to contact the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, which was Palma, how would they identify their respective units in the radio transmission, generally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: They would refer to those units in radio communication as Palma and Zlatar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, let's even narrow the focus of your testimony down a little bit more, and I'd like you to describe in precision how you and your unit actually captured radio communications. Starting at the point in time when you're sitting at a monitor with a set of headphones listening, tell us what you would do you from that point in time until the point in time when the radio communication had been reduced to writing and transmitted on to your superior headquarters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I apologise, but do you mean from the moment I put the headphones on onwards? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: So from the moment I put my headset on, whether it is me or any of the other operators, we would wait for the participants to start communicating, and when they do, we immediately switch on the tape recorder and listen to the message. As soon as it is over, it is transcribed onto a piece of paper, which means from the sound record to a visual record, and then this is taken to another room where that is typed out and sent on to the main headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You told us earlier in your testimony, Witness U, that you and your unit had been up at the mountaintop listening to Bosnian Serb military communications for two years. Can you tell us, based on your experience, whether you were able to identify the specific speakers in some of the radio communications that you intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to do so; extremely well, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you intercepted the communication, was the intercepted communication on a tape recording?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it was recorded on tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you earlier testified about you and your men going to reduce the intercepted communication to writing, did that mean that the intercept operator would again listen to the tape carefully and write down exactly the communication that he had intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. It's not always simple to do. Sometimes there are problems when you're trying to transcribe these tapes because the quality may not always be very good because of the poor connection established which we managed to intercept. Then there are difficulties, so you have to rewind it back and forth several times. You even have to ask the assistance of other people who may know the voice better so as to make sure that the message is taken down correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you on occasion listen to these intercepted radio communications time and time again in order to ensure that they are accurately transcribed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, besides the ability to recognise the speakers, the people who were speaking on these radio communications, were there other ways that you and your men could identify who was communicating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: They would sometimes give their names themselves, and then the orders, judging from the orders, one could gather who was ordering whom, and from that one would know who was the most important participant. Then came the voice, then the other code names used, and all these little pieces are put together like a jigsaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, where were the handwritten notes of the intercepted communication placed? You said pieces of paper. What kind of paper were they placed on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: These were notebooks with some kind of a marking on them, at least a number, and the numbers would be in order, and many of them would have an indication of the type of equipment used to record and transcribe. Some notebooks would have additional information; for instance, messages in written form such as signatures, then the code name under which a document was sent to us, then the date when the notebook first started to be used, and the contents would be inside, the contents of intercepted radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, before we get to the actual examination of these notebooks, I want to continue with the procedure for just a minute. After the radio communication was written down in the notebook, what was the next step in the procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: When the message was taken down in the notebook, the next step would be to take that notebook to the computer, to enter it into the computer. As soon as it has been typed, making sure that no changes need to be made, that it is reliable, it is sent to the command of my unit, to the headquarters of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a number of copies from notebooks and they're going to be in binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours should have binders, at least three binders of these notebooks. Before I begin this examination, I will inform Your Honours how these notebooks are organised for ease of reference. These binders have tabs in them and behind each tab is a copy of an individual notebook. The original notebooks, which I will make available to Your Honours to inspect, are here. In fact, I would invite Your Honours to inspect one or two of the originals, although we would like to maintain the copies of the originals as evidence. These are true copies. But this witness will be able to identify specific notebooks in the three volumes, and I'm going to now ask him to examine, with the assistance of the usher, certain exhibits contained in these notebooks. Mr. Usher, will you turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 279 and show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, the usher will open up the notebook and show you tab 1, Prosecutor's Exhibit 279. Would you quickly inspect that exhibit, Witness U, and let me ask you, is this a notebook that was prepared by your unit? If so, can you tell the Judges how you know that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: This is a notebook from our location that we used. I can recognise my handwriting, "REU 128," and there are 52 persons mentioned, and there is my signature. I can even see text written in my own hand inside the notebook --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: -- and there are other indications by which I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You've examined the original of that notebook in my office prior to coming here to testify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, does this particular notebook contain the intercepted conversations that were recorded by members of your staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it does. This can be seen from the handwriting that I can recognise. The way in which we marked these messages, we had a unified manner. Then the frequency, the order, the participants we intercepted, the participants from our own area of responsibility. So this is our notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the written records of each intercepted communication that are contained in that notebook, were they made at or about the time you actually intercepted the communication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, at the exact time or round about the exact time that the interception took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do those written records of each intercepted communication consist of a verbatim recording of the intercepted communication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were these notebooks, such as Exhibit 279, kept by the army as part of their regular business?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go through this exercise with you now for a series of other notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I also have some of the originals, which I'm prepared to pass up to Your Honours. It may be of assistance to you. Frankly, it gives a better flavour of what these notebooks consist of. I'll make them available to my colleagues as well. But if I could pass two or three exemplars up to Your Honours now, then I could continue with this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, while the Judges and Defence counsel are examining the original copies of these notebooks, if you would turn your attention briefly to Prosecutor's Exhibit 280, which will be the next item I'm going to be asking you about. The usher will assist you. If you would inspect Exhibit 280, Witness U, and I would ask you if you could identify that as a notebook that was also from your unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have counsel and Your Honours had sufficient time to examine the original notebooks? And if so, I'll continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, is Exhibit 280 a notebook that was taken by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Document 280 is also a document kept by the representatives of my unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And again does that accurately reflect the substance of the conversations that were intercepted by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do those notes accurately verbatim contain the intercepted communication or the parts of the intercepted communication as heard on the radio transmission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, this notebook and all of the notebooks I'm going to be asking you about were maintained by the army in the regular course of their business; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could you turn your attention to the next notebook, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 282. Witness U, we're going to go through this same exercise with a number of these notebooks. If you could just tell me if this was a notebook that was maintained by your unit, prepared by your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Turn to the next exhibit, please, 283. Would you inspect that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll say for the record, Mr. President and Your Honours, I've shown the witness the original notebooks of each of these exhibits I'm going to be identifying, and they are an exact copy. But I think it is necessary for the witness to make that representation to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: This too is a document that was compiled in my unit at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that's an exact copy of the original; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 284, which is the next exhibit. Can you identify that notebook as a notebook that was prepared by either you or members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That document was prepared by my unit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take a look at the next exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 285, please. Is that a notebook, Witness U, 285, that is prepared by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is the notebook prepared by members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 287, please. Is this a notebook that was prepared by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that too is a document prepared by my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 288, please. Witness U, is Prosecutor's Exhibit 288 a notebook that was prepared by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 290, please. Would you inspect that and tell us whether that is a notebook that was also prepared by members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lastly, would you take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 294, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. That too is the document from my unit, compiled at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So all of the documents that I've just shown you, all of those exhibits you've been able to identify as coming from your unit by either recognising the handwriting of your colleagues or recognising your own entries in them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in respect of each of these notebooks, each of these notebooks contain the accurate recording of intercepted radio communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I don't know when Your Honours want a break, if this is the appropriate time. I don't have too much more for this witness, but we're going to go into specific conversations next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon, I think that this is a very good time to take a break. We'll have a 20-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We apologise for the delay. Perhaps I should speak in English. [In English] I must say that maybe we will change "blind" from a noun to an adjective to qualify its behaviour. It is something ridiculous to have all this time, 25 minutes, because of this problem. So I think it's necessary to pay attention to this, and I ask the registrar to refer this problem to the Registrar. Okay? [Interpretation] We are now going to continue. Mr. Harmon, it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. I'm going to focus the attention of the witness on two conversations that are found in the notebooks that he specifically listened to and recorded. The first of those is found, Your Honours, for your reference, in Prosecutor's Exhibit 279, and it is found at page 00778904. I've marked in the exhibit copy of the exhibit the reference so I could show it to the witness. Mr. Usher, we have an independent copy of just this conversation. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 301-1C. If the first page of the Bosnian copy could be placed on the ELMO, just the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone, please, Mr. Harmon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could place the first page, the excerpt on the ELMO, not the second page because the witness is identified by his initials at the end of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, Witness U, the conversation that you see on the monitor in front of you, is that the same conversation that appears in Prosecutor's Exhibit 279, which is in front of you in the binder? Did you understand my question? Maybe you didn't hear it. Let me repeat my question because I don't think you could hear it. Is the exhibit that is on the monitor in front of you a copy of the page that's marked in Prosecutor's Exhibit 279?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you reduce the tone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you take a look at the exhibit that is in the binder, 279, at page 00778904. Let me ask you, is this a conversation -- strike that. Is the handwriting on this exhibit your handwriting? I think the binder keeps turning off the earphones for this witness so he can't hear my questions. Let me ask you once again, Witness U --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- the handwriting in the notebook, which is found at page 00778904 and 8905, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this a conversation that you personally intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this an intercepted communication that you then reduced to writing in the notebook, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 279?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The language booth should have the English and a French translation of this particular exhibit, and I think for purposes of making the procedure more efficient I'm going to ask the language booth merely to translate the exhibit that's on the ELMO. They have copies of the official language translations, and if they can just read the translations into the record, we can then turn to the next exhibit. For the benefit of the language service people, the English translation is 301-1A and the French translation of the exhibit that's on the ELMO is 301-1B. So if those could be read into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we suggest that the witness read it out in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. I'm suggesting that the language booth, which has a copy of the translation provided to it by the Office of the Prosecutor, merely read the translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [as read] Just a moment, to Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you start in the upper left-hand corner which indicates a series of numbers and channels and time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [as read] 7847 - channel 5 - 2056 hours. Major-General Zivanovic - X. X: Just a moment, to Colonel Vukovic. /as written/ M: Good evening. X: Evening. M: How's it going? X: We are fine, how about you? M: How can I find out where General Zivanovic is? I've been waiting here for him on his orders since 1700 hours. X: He's here. M: What? X: He's here. M: There? X: Yes. M: Well, put me through to him. X: I'll try now. Z: Yes? M: Good evening. Z: Good evening, Vuko. M: Things are all right, good, here. I did everything in the spirit of what I received last night. And in morning /?he/ called me Natasku /word unknown/ and I came here this morning at around 10 o'clock and I /as written/. Z: Major! M: Yes, yes, I understand you. Z: I just came from the checkpoint. M: Could you repeat that, please? Z: I said that paper which was sent - there is one - from Blagojevic, about me. M: OK. Z: Read my conclusions. M: I understand. Z: Because (from here on drowned out by previously recorded conversation) M: I understand, completely, and then we'll focus on the one down there (drowned out again by previously recorded conversation). M: I understand. I'm going to put my post up there. Z: Listen. Where up there are your boys? M: Well, my boys are now in the western part, working there as of today. Everything's in place, sweet as a nut. Z: Excellent. M: I did that today. Z: ... (mumbles something short). M: I understand. Z: Take care. M: Take care.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please don't read the signature and the initials that are associated with this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness U, who is "Z" in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It is "Z", and in this conversation it was General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You told us in your earlier examination that after a conversation was handwritten into a notebook, it was then typed, and a typed copy of the conversation was forwarded on up your chain of command. Let me show you the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the B/C/S version, first of all, could be shown to the witness so he can inspect it. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 301-2B. If that could be shown to the witness so he could look at it himself, and then we'll place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, would you inspect that, Witness U. Witness U, is this the typed version of the intercepted communication that was prepared by you or by a member of your unit and then forwarded up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document typed out in our unit and forwarded up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was that document prepared on the same day that the conversation that has just been read into the record was intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what date, then, looking at this document, was it that the conversation that was just read into the record -- what date was it intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: On the first document, there's no date. On the second, there is a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so what is that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. We've finished with this particular document. We'll turn to another conversation. For Your Honours' reference, this next conversation is found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 280, and it is found at page 00779705. Witness U, I've marked that with a yellow tab for your ease of reference in Prosecutor's Exhibit 280. Mr. Usher, if you could kindly place the first page of the B/C/S version, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 302-1C, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness U, you have the actual copy of the notebook, Prosecutor's Exhibit 280, in front of you and the conversation I've just referred to. Now, would you examine the conversation that's in the notebook and the conversation that is on the monitor in front of you, and are they the same conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, they are the same conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this a conversation -- first of all, is this your handwriting on the page 00779705?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this is your handwriting in 302-1C as well, the version that's on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this a conversation that you personally intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you faithfully record from the tape to the notebook the contents of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could follow the same procedure that we did before, if I could ask the language booths to translate this document. I will give you the numbers. The English translation for this document is 302-1A, and the French version is 302-1B. If we could start in the same procedure that we did before and if it could be completely read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [as read] At 2102 hours, 784.7 MHz, Channel 3. Priority. Palma Duty Officer (Major Jokic) - Badem - X - Y. : Hello, Badem. Let me talk to Beara. B: Who wants to talk to him? : The Palma duty officer wants to talk to him. Beara is needed urgently, somebody needs him. The Superior Command urgently needs him, but he has to call me. B: Okay. P: Okay, what? Give me Beara. Don't hang up. J: Hello, who is it, Major, I'm the duty officer at Palma. I need Beara urgently. This is Major Jokic. Who is that? Why the fuck are you not answering? Is Ostoja there? Is Brko there? Don't fuck around. The line has to be free, and you must pick it up right away. Who is Ostoja? Is Ostoja there? Have him call me urgently. I will, I will. Hello, hello. B: Here is Beara, you have him on the line. J: Hello. X: Hello. Is the operations duty officer looking for me? Go ahead. Vojanovic is not here, he is up at Snagovo. There are some problems there, at the line I've told you about. The Turks have pushed our guys back towards Crni Vrh. Y: ... X: Yes. I told him to consolidate the lines up there. That's it. J: Hello. B: Just a moment. One moment old man. J: Is that Beara? Jokic here. BE: ... J: We were together, Colonel, sir. Number 155 called you and asked you to call him urgently. BE: ... J: Number 155. That's, I mean, Superior Command, you go ahead and call them, you have, so I don't speak like this. BE: ... J: Yes. Hey. We have huge problems over here. BE: ... J: There are big problems. Well with the people, I mean, with the parcel. BE: ... J: Who? Drago is nowhere around. I don't know where the others are all day. BE: ... J: What? Call up there number 155 in the Superior Command and that's it. Okay, boss. BE: ... Why number 155? Where is that? J: Well, I can't tell you on this line, you know. You have it over there at the signalmen, who that is. BE: Yes? J: Bye. Remark: Thanks to the switchboard operator's mistake at Badem, we recorded a conversation between "X" and "Y", who couldn't be heard, while he was intercepting and the line 44 was open for Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, let me ask you some specific questions about this intercepted communication. First let me refer you to the terms "Palma" and "duty officer". You earlier testified about code names. Palma was associated with what location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Palma was the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Badem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Badem was the Drina Corps. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can refer to one of the maps. It's been many years. If you would like to refer to either the Prosecutor's Exhibit 137, which is the large board, or the green map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In this conversation, next to a speaker there are dots. What do the dots represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The dots represent something that was either not heard, that was poorly heard, or that was unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So where you couldn't understand or couldn't hear it, you inserted dots in order to maintain the accuracy of what you could, in fact, hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. Only the things that we were sure of were put down on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, looking at the handwritten document that's in front of you, the notebook version of this conversation, is there any date when this particular conversation was intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: There's no date on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me focus your attention on part of your earlier testimony when you said there was a group of other people who were intercepting communications from the location where your group was located, that is, a group from the State Security Service. Did you and the State Security Service share the information that you had intercepted on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, we would pass on our information to that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would they prepare a report containing the information that you had shared with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, they did prepare a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And have you seen copies of their reports that they would forward to their higher command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 302-2C, the four-page document. If you can identify it, I would appreciate it. If you can't, just tell me you can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If that could be given to the witness so he can inspect. If you could turn to the last page of that document. It should be a four-page document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same document that I have in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let me just ask you some questions. If not, I'll proceed with this document through another witness. Have you ever seen this type of a document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I won't ask any additional questions on this document. I have another witness who will come in and identify this document. I have no additional questions of this witness. Thank you very much, Mr. President and Your Honours. Thank you, Witness U. The Defence will ask you questions next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Petrusic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness U. The unit (redacted) belonged or was subordinated to the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness U, before I pass on to my next question, as both of us speak the same language, please be so kind as to make a short pause after my question of 10 to 15 seconds for the benefit of the interpreters. At the location where your unit was stationed, was a unit of the 21st Division also stationed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your unit and the unit of the 21st Division, were they coordinated or, rather, did they have a single command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: For me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you were under the command of the 2nd Corps, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did these two units coordinate their activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was your equipment placed in the same room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you act on the basis of the same documents? Were your basic procedures the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I don't know how they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that the basic documents regulating electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare, orders for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare, document 1, and document 2, the plan for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare, are they one and the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand your question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have orders in the form of documents for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have a plan for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Not in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your superior commander from the 2nd Corps, did he issue you such a plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It is sufficient to say that we had orders. The plan is not important in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to answer my question, please. You said there was no plan in written form. Does that imply that it was issued orally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It implies no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the premises in which you worked, did you act, allow me to call it, "conditionally" on the basis of rules for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I don't know which rules you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have any rules drawn up by a higher command, any normative procedures which guided your operations on the basis of which you acted? As a member of the former Yugoslav army in which you acquired your knowledge and special training as a radio telegraph operator, you know that in those areas action is regulated by rules which represent a military secret of the highest confidentiality. So my question is: Did your unit have such rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I do not agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question. Did you have rules on the basis of which you operated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have a logbook, a diary, for the station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Not in the form that you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did your rules stipulate that such a diary be kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you in any way whatsoever keep records of any kind as to the number of shifts and number of individuals manning those shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you took over a shift from a previous shift, did you conduct this handing-over process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You, (redacted), did you sign a paper of any kind to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of paper you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the leader coming on duty and the leader going off duty would hand over their affairs to the next shift and shift leader, would they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And they did this according to a certain procedure. They would keep records and inform each other of what had happened in the previous shift, and possibly give instructions or guidelines to the shift coming on duty stipulating the frequencies that attention should be paid to in particular.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes. This handover of shift duty was done by the commander of the company or the authorised individual in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: All these records would go to the higher command, would they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The notebooks that were mentioned, the originals that have been presented by the Prosecutor and the photocopies which are authentic representations of the originals, who supplied you with those notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The notebooks came from the 2nd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether it was the duty -- that is to say, whether those notebooks, at the end, on the last page, would they have a stamp of the command who issued them to you, with a stamp of the unit in charge, in whose safekeeping that notebook has been placed, and that it should be paginated? Do you know about all that, that procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I am not of the same opinion as you in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: May we say that the notebooks that came from the superior command did not contain stamps either of your unit or the superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: They did not have a stamp, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we say that they were not paginated either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Well, I don't agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I have just one moment, please. We received these documents just before the beginning of the proceedings, and glancing through them, we were able to note that most of these notebooks do not have pages on them, are not numbered. So may we just have a look at them, and then I will be presenting them to the witness. I'll retract that question and return to it later on for technical reasons, not to waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next question is the following: At the end of each notebook, was there your signature certifying that the notebook has so many pages, and was your signature at the end of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, not every notebook had my signature at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look now at 282, Exhibit 282, please. It is Prosecution Exhibit 282.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I apologise for interrupting, but perhaps you could ask the witness the questions, because otherwise you might get answers like, "I'm not of your opinion," "I don't agree with you," and so on, so perhaps it would be a better way to ask a direct question and the answer will be yes or no or something along those lines. But please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 282, take a look at that please, and I'll go back to my previous question. The pages of this notebook have not been numbered.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I apologise. Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The pages on this notebook do not have numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Exhibit 288 is the next document I'd like you to look at. Do the pages of that notebook have numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No, this notebook does not have page numbers either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: While you were at Okresanica, did you have those two notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We received them, we used them, and we sent them back, if that's your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you got through a whole notebook -- could you explain the procedure to us -- did you send it to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: I apologise again, but I say that I got the notebook from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you when the notebook has -- once it had been filled out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: At the first next shift change, the notebook would go back to the command again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me now go back to some technical questions on the technical side of your work, your profession. When you put your headsets on and you intercept a conversation, you're following on one channel. How many participants can you intercept and hear on that one channel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Two participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you hear both of them equally well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Usually, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is there a rule of some kind as to which person you can hear better, the one calling up or the one being called? And, please, could you refrain from smiling. I am asking you whether the recipient of the call is heard better or the caller.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: In this case, it is the caller. Just one moment, please. The radio relay station to which our antennae is directed, whose transmitter it is on that frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness U, glancing through the notebooks that you prepared, we can see that they all have frequencies and the time. There is no date; that is to say, not on every occasion. Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There is no date for each conversation because the reports to the Superior Command were sent in the form of daily bulletins, and so in each of these reports -- each of these reports contain the dates, but the notebook is the origin, the source, and we considered that to be -- we did not consider it to be compulsory, because the main document for us was actually the report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the duty operator places the date on the daily report that he sends to the corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If the daily report is sent by the operator, does that daily report -- that is to say, at the end of that daily report, does he place a stamp which states the day and the time when the telegram was sent, and on the other side the day and time -- date and time when the telegram was received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Sir, the reports were sent out daily. As to the date, the computer had a date in it, because that is how the reports were transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The audio cassettes, audiotapes doing the recording, were they stored -- that is to say, were they handed over to the Superior Command as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know the fate of those tapes, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No. I would be given an empty tape, and I would send out a full tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: For you to intercept two parties in a conversation, how many sets of devices did you need?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: One set was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: With this one set, were you able to intercept and follow one channel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, I have no further questions. Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Two brief areas I would like to explore with Witness U.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness U, in your direct examination you testified that your area of responsibility for your unit was the area that was bordered by the Sava, the Drina, and the Bosna Rivers. That's quite a large area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Also there has been reference made to the 21st Division, Anti-Electronic Warfare Division, being a unit that was physically at or near your location but didn't work with your specific unit. My question is this: Did the 21st Division, Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit, focus on a specific area that was contained within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what area did they focus on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: It was a more narrow area, the Posavina region and perhaps a little further afield as well. You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Posavina area was north in your area of responsibility; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the area of Srebrenica and the area where the Zvornik Brigade operated was more to the south, the southern part of your area of responsibility; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, my colleague asked you a number of questions about the dating of reports, and earlier I had shown you -- and I'd like to have this placed back on the ELMO, please -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 301-2B. Now, we had earlier examined the page from a notebook dealing with this very conversation. That was found at Exhibit 301-1C, for the record. The exhibit that's on the ELMO now, Witness U, you indicated earlier in your examination that this exhibit represented the typewritten version of the conversation found in the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the report, in typewritten form, that was then forwarded to your command; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if that could be moved down on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, you'll see two lines. One says "Broj 626", and the other says "Dana" with some numbers following it. What are those numbers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: That is the number of the document we sent out, and underneath, the date when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These types of documents such as in this exhibit were sent out on a daily basis to your higher command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On occasion, were such reports sent more than one time a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, in the period when there were frequent operations on the radio devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, for example, during the period of Srebrenica, was that a period of intense and high activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that was the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so were a number of these typewritten reports sent to your command, more than one a day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: In this case, probably, yes. That is to say, yes, more than once a day, but I don't know whether this occurred every day during these activities. But during that activity, they were sent out several times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Actually, I withdraw the question. I have no additional questions, Mr. President. Witness U, thank you kindly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions? No. Judge Wald? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, I would like to ask you two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a first question for you to clarify matters. What was the date when you started your military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Your Honours, the date I joined the ranks of the Yugoslav People's Army was the 6th of April, 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because we heard "1992".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely why I asked the question, Judge. My next question: You said that at the end of your work, that is to say, there was a third entity between two communicating peoples, so the caller, the receiver, and this was the type of radio communication employed. I should like -- that is to say, part of your work was anti-electronic warfare. How many devices did you actually have, if you can answer that question for me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mean how many sets of equipment we had or how many devices? I think you probably mean the number of devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of devices.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: The number of devices was over 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many people could work at the same time with one and the same apparatus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you're asking about the devices, then one man works on one device. But the situation is different if we're talking about sets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One device could intercept different frequencies or just one single frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: One device would listen to several channels on one band, in one direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said that you could listen better to transmitters which, how shall I put it, which were -- to which your antenna was directed.
