So if you directed your antenna towards your transmitter, you could listen to that transmitter better, you could hear it better; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Usually we would hear the participant better whose receiver we would listen to because that participant was facing the same problems that we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So does that mean that in the transcripts of the recordings, there are many things left out; that is to say, that at that point in time you did not manage to hear well. Is that what we can gather from this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U
utterances.text: We did not manage to understand at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Witness, I think we have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming here. We wish you a safe journey home. Don't move, please, because you are under protective measures, and I suggest to the parties that we now have a break so that the witness may leave and have the other witness brought in. Mr. Harmon, is the next witness protected as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next witness is protected, Mr. President. Also we have some exhibits to regulate with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, that's true. Regarding the exhibits, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. We would move into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 138, which is a map; Prosecutor's Exhibit 300, which is a list of intercept operators, and we would ask that that be under seal; Prosecutor's Exhibit 139, which is a green map with communication lines on it; Prosecutor's 137, which is the VRS code names; and then we have a series of notebooks, Prosecutor's Exhibits 279, 280, 282, 283, 284, 285, 287, 288, 290, 294, and we would ask that all of those exhibits be under seal because they contain the identities of this protected witness and other protected witnesses who will be testifying in the immediate future; then we have Prosecutor's Exhibit 301-1A, B, and C, which is an intercepted communication taken by this witness; and 302A, B, and C, which is a second intercepted communication taken by this witness. There are French and English versions with each of those. I believe that is the list of the exhibits. I should add, I would ask that 301-1A, B, and C and 301-2A and B be under seal as well as they will identify this witness by the initials that are attached on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I see that Exhibits 281, 286, 289, and 291 to 293, you are not moving them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. We will lay the foundation for those notebooks, which essentially were from a different location, through a different witness. I would like to add one additional exhibit I see on the chart. It is 302-1A, B, and C, if I haven't mentioned that already, and 302-2A, B, and C, again asking that those be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, allow me briefly to say something, hoping that I will not be misunderstood. In the course of the last hearings, when we received exhibits, we suggested to the Chamber and you agreed with us at the time that this case -- in this case too, we are receiving a large quantity of material and we would appeal to the Chamber to give us time, until the end of this sitting, which I think is the end of July, for us to be able to express our opinion regarding the admission of these exhibits. Regardless of whether there will be any objections or not, the Defence will certainly not recall the witnesses in question. So that would be our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree we have had this discussion before. There are large volumes of evidence that we will be tendering in this session and in the next session. We have advised the Defence in writing, and I have advised them orally, I've invited them to apply the Rules of this Tribunal specifically to engage in reciprocal discovery. We have provided to the Defence in a timely fashion all of the exhibits that we're obligated to do so. I've informed them that there are a large number of documents that we are going to maintain, and if they would like to see them, they should ask to see them and we will engage in reciprocal discovery. With all due respect to my colleague, if they find themselves at any disadvantage it's of their own making. We certainly believe that these exhibits should be admitted now. The foundation for them has been laid. The witness who is here in respect of each of these conversations and each of the notebooks which he's identified has testified before this Chamber. If, at a later time, after these documents have been admitted, the Defence wants to challenge these documents on some other basis other than the basis which this witness has testified about, they can do that in their case. But I believe at this point in time the foundation for each of these documents has been laid, and we would urge the Court to admit them into evidence at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Certainly, Mr. Harmon, there's no question that you have communicated in a timely fashion and in appropriate form, but in any event, Mr. Petrusic tells us that he needs to review those documents, and to do so he needs a little more time. This does not entail the possibility of recalling the witness. So the question is whether or not you agree that we can discuss the admission of these exhibits later, that is, to give some additional time to Mr. Petrusic to review those exhibits and state his position regarding their admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Our position is, Your Honour, that the appropriate foundation has been laid now. If my colleague needs additional time to review them, certainly he has them in his possession. I don't mean to in any way obstruct the process, but I believe that the foundation for these documents has been laid now. Mr. Petrusic, even if they're admitted, has them in his possession and he can review them at a later time. But we would, once again, renew our application for admission of the documents at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, leaving for a moment the Rule on reciprocal discovery aside, isn't it possible, with such a large volume of material, for the Defence to get it a couple of days ahead of time or something so that this -- because it is kind of hard to take three volumes and run through them here. I know your argument, I understand it, on reciprocal discovery but I'm not convinced that that opportunity rules out their having some reasonable period to look through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Wald, the documents that are before Your Honours, there are a number of volumes of the notebooks that are -- they have available to them before we're offering them into evidence. So in part, the area that you've addressed is met. In respect of the other concern, Your Honour, we have made our position and repeated our position. Perhaps counsel and I can sit down and reach an agreement, and we will attempt to do so, but I want to repeat that I've advised the Defence on a number of occasions, both in writing and orally, that there are large volumes of documents that are coming their way and they have been fully apprised of that and have elected consciously to not invoke the Rule which would permit them to see the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Does that mean that your having informed them that a large number is coming, they couldn't look at them a couple of days ahead of time, or a day ahead of time, have access to them without the reciprocal discovery Rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think we can find an accommodation, Judge Wald. I think we will; we just have to sit down and talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is granting the necessary time to the Defence to review the documents. I think you asked until the end of this month, of June. Therefore, you will have this additional time to review the documents, and after that the Chamber will make a determination regarding the admission of documents into evidence. So now we're going to have -- Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I accept the Court's ruling, obviously, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, you cannot accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But we accept the Court's ruling, Your Honour. I only draw attention to the possibility that depending on whatever questions the Defence poses at a later time, we may be required to call back this witness or the successive witnesses that we have. So that remains a possibility depending on the questions that are raised by the Defence. I point that out. I hope it doesn't come to pass but it's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The Defence pointed out that he will not return to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He may not need to, but depending on the questions he raises, Judge Riad, we may wish to resolve the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I would hope that you will not see our ruling as ruling out for future admissions your sitting down with Defence counsel and see if they get it a day or two ahead of time that they won't -- because otherwise I can understand your problem of waiting until the end of the month and then having a lot of things at the end of the month. I think the better way would be, after this ruling, is if you give them time so they can make their objections at the time of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. The decision has been made, and we are going to decide to have a half-hour break too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Are you comfortable, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher is going to show you a piece of paper with your name written on it. Tell us, yes or no, is that indeed your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now you're going to answer questions which Mr. Cayley is going to put to you, who is on your right. Mr. Cayley, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, learned Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I shall call you "Witness V" during your evidence in order to protect your identity, and if you could remember not to mention any names of your colleagues while you are testifying, in order to ensure their security as well. My first question: What nationality are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is your faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In what years did you do your regular military service in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In which unit of the JNA did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: In the Anti-Aircraft Defence Regiment, I was a signalsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were a signaller, a signalman. Can you explain to the Judges what that involved and what type of skills you learned in the JNA as a signaller?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: They are the duties of a signalman. I was taught to use radio equipment, on conduct in radio communications, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At what level of headquarters did you work as a signaller?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: At the level of regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where was the communications equipment located that you worked on within the regiment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It was at Vozra.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the regiment have a command vehicle in which communications equipment was installed, and that's where you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in order to move forward quickly in time, I think you left the JNA in May of 1992, and you eventually returned to Tuzla, arriving in Tuzla in August of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What unit of the Bosnian army did you join in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Electronic Reconnaissance and Anti-Electronic Warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, just one point. You're using some technical terms, and you speak very quickly. So if you could try and speak a little more slowly, that would make the lives of the interpreters easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 138 could be placed on the ELMO, please. Now, while the exhibit is being placed on the ELMO -- that's actually the small map, the small version of the map that's here, Mr. Usher. I have a spare. It's just easier for the witness if it's on the ELMO rather than here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, whereabouts was this unit located in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Majevica Mountain, the location called Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just look at the map next to you and point to the Judges the location of your unit when you joined it in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating the green circle marked "Okresanica" on Prosecutor's Exhibit 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you know, to whom was your unit directly subordinated in the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: To the command of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges very briefly what your responsibility was as a soldier within this unit at Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I worked there as a radio surveyor using the equipment. My responsibilities -- we would be divided into shifts of six hours each, and that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've stated that your responsibility was as a radio surveyor. Can you explain to the Judges the process that you went through?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 298 and 299, that might assist him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you could explain to the Judges, as you sat down in front of your equipment, the process that you went through in order to monitor radio transmissions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Taking over duties when my shift started, we would receive instructions from colleagues who worked in the previous shift on the intensity of communications, the type of communications, everything that had happened in the previous shift. We would take our seats at the equipment, at the devices. We would monitor everything. And when a conversation was aired, we had tape recorders for recording. We would switch them on. We would intercept the conversation, then transcribe it, and that was our duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could put 298 back on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, could you identify this equipment for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It's amateur equipment, readjusted for the work we did. These are amateur apparatuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this the equipment which you listened to these radio transmissions on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the next exhibit, which is 299, could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It's an Uher tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How was it possible to record conversations from the receiver onto the tape recorder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: They were connected with cables.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain the process of transcription to the Judges, the process that you went through when you transcribed a conversation from a tape onto paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: When a conversation has been recorded, the tape would be rewound to the beginning of the conversation, and then that conversation would begin to be transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What would happen if there was anything you couldn't hear properly on the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: If we couldn't hear something, then a couple of colleagues would come and then we would try to decipher it together, and if we didn't succeed, then we would put dots to indicate that that part of the conversation was unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it possible to identify the participants in any conversation that you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly they themselves would give their names. We recognised some of them but it was not up to us to say who they were. In most cases they identified themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, principally, whose military communications were you listening to? Which party to the conflict were you listening to at Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, once you had transcribed a conversation from a tape yourself, what happened to that written record that you had made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It would be forwarded to the command, and therefore further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In what form was it forwarded to the higher command, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: In the form of typed reports on the computer. If something was particularly important, then it would be reported immediately by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you stated in your evidence that you would produce a written form of the conversation, and you now state that a typed form of the conversation went to the higher command. So another soldier was involved in the process of making that typed report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to explain that when transcribing the conversation, it was first in my handwriting and then he would copy it out on the computer, this other soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of what happened to the tapes that you used on the tape machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Many tapes, because they were in short supply, were used several times over, so I don't know what happened to them. I think they were all taped over.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The procedure that you've just explained to the Judges is the procedure that you went through throughout your time of duty. You repeated this process throughout your time of duty at Okresanica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you were working at Okresanica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the Court's information, Your Honours, the name of this witness appears on the list which the previous witness actually placed before the Court. It's Exhibit 300 and he's on that exhibit. I won't show it to the witness. If Prosecutor's Exhibit 313C could be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, what I would like you to do now, and we've already discussed this, is to identify conversations which you took down at or about the period of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If 313 could be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is an extract from a notebook and we'll talk about the notebooks in a moment. Do you recognise your handwriting on those two pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this a conversation that you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that could now be placed on the ELMO, and if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 279. Exhibit 279, Your Honours, is the complete notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in fact, Prosecutor's Exhibit 279 is a book that was numbered at the time, and if you look in the top right-hand corner, rather than me using the Tribunal's evidence registration numbers which are long, if you turn to page 31, and you can see the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can assist the witness. Your Honours, the ERN number is 00778878; there is a "31" in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the conversation which you've just identified, can you see it within this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just for confirmation, is that page 31, if you look at the top right-hand corner of that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has identified that the previous conversation is contained within Prosecutor's Exhibit 279 at pages 00778877 and 00778878.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated earlier, Witness, that often the participants in conversations identified themselves. Is this particular conversation an example of that, or at least an indication of the unit that was involved in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges why that's so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Most probably they did not abide by radio communications rules, or they didn't know that we were listening in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the identification within this particular intercept? What is the word that identifies the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It is the secret name Zlatar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, if you can from memory, what the call sign "Zlatar" means? What military unit does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It is the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate actually reading this out myself, if that is all right, rather than asking the interpreters to do it. I'll read the official English translation, which is 313/A. The particular intercept is titled "785.000 MHz, Channel 5, 1345 hours." "Duty operations officer - Zlatar /code-name/ Z: Hello. O: Yes. Z: This is Zlatar. Tell me, are there any complications over there at the connection with the 4th Battalion, with those boys? O: /? They advanced about ten miles /crossed out: 1447 hours, channel 5/ O: Hello. Nothing has been /illegible/ Z: Yes. O: And /illegible/, whatever happened happened. Z: I have some information that there was some /illegible/ between my /unit/ and you guys. O: Well, there was. Z: Well, there was for example towards Konjevic Polje and Kosprat /as written/ stop. O: We have no information that it's like that /as written/ Z: What have you done there? O: Well, listen. It's been determined here ... and still nothing happens to anybody. Z: ... the forward command post there. O: Please, I can just put you through /? up there/ to General Krstic. He's in charge of this attack." And then there is in brackets that the conversation breaks off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, towards the end of this conversation, there are a number of dots that you referred to. Does that indicate words that clearly couldn't be heard in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could go to the beginning of this journal, in fact the second page, and there's a date. Do you see a date written there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the date that's written there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 26th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could go to the second-to-last page of this journal, Mr. Usher. It's the page with the table full of numbers on it, the numbers irrelevant, part of the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There's a date at the top of that page, Witness, with "A/A" written on it. What is the date and what does "A/A" mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It means "Ad Acta", end of diary, 24th of July, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said "the 24th of July". Can you look at the number again? Is it a "4" or a "7"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Sorry, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, there's a misunderstanding. Is it a "4" or is it a "7"? Is it "27" or "24"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So would it be correct to say that the conversation that we've just referred to was taken down at some time between the 26th of June, 1995, which is the date at the beginning of this book, and the date of the last entry or the filing of this diary on the 27th of July, 1995, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And can you be any more specific about the date in respect of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: At the beginning of every day, the date would be indicated usually when we started working, and so the intercepts for that day can be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You and I have already looked in this booklet, and in this particular case the date was not written at the beginning of the shift; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that exceptional, do you think? Was the normal process to write the date at the beginning of every shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It was customary, but it happened that it was left out. That depended on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move to the next exhibit, which is 314, and if the witness could be shown 314C. Mr. Usher, if you could put it in front of the witness, to start with, before on the ELMO so he can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you look through that, Witness, and see if you recognise that particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this an intercept that you transcribed from a tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now, Mr. Usher, we could go back to page 31 of Exhibit 279.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you look on that page and, I think, the following pages and see whether or not the intercept that you've just looked at as an extract is actually contained within the notebook. Look at all of the pages, just to make sure. Is that the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I'm not going to read all of this document. The witness has laid the foundation. But I am going to read, from the English version, at the bottom of page 2, because that's actually important for the next intercept, for the identification of the next intercept. So I'm reading now from the bottom of page 2, where it begins: "C: Just a moment. Hello. My boys here are looking for Zlatar Duty Operations Officer. Is that you? X: I'm not, but I'm here. C: Could you call them? X: Yes. Z: Hello. This is Krstic. X: This is Komjenovic. Go ahead, General, Sir. K: I asked to be put through to Krsmanovic. Is he there? X: /illegible/ Krsmanovic isn't here, but I assume ... down you have to /call/ again. K: Come on, put me through to him again, Zlatar."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Again, Witness, we won't belabour the point, but this is an intercept that was taken from the same booklet as the last one, which has a beginning date of 26 June 1995 and an end date of 24 July 1995; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So would it be safe to say that you took this intercept down sometime between the 26th of June, 1995 and the 24th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if we can move to the next exhibit, which is 315.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could read that through, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: [As read] General Krstic/X/ - Krsmanovic/Y/. X: What's happened with the buses? Y: ... X: Start out immediately, and they should do the same. Y: /inaudible/. X: Hey, do you understand "immediately"? They should start immediately. Y: /inaudible/. X: Come on. Y: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, how were you able to identify General Krstic as "X" and Krsmanovic as "Y"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Because both names begin with a "K" so this was to differentiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The question that I have for you, and it refers to the previous conversation which I read out, how were you able to identify "X" as General Krstic and "Y" as Krsmanovic on the radio net?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: From the previous conversation, the one that you read out. This is just a continuation of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That was the conversation in which General Krstic identified himself and specifically asked for Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Mr. Usher, you could go to page 34 in Exhibit 279. That, I think, actually demonstrates the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you look at page 34 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 279, Witness. The conversation in the top left-hand corner, is that the same conversation that you have just read out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could go back to the previous page, page 33, which is the previous conversation which I read out, in the bottom right-hand corner, is that where General Krstic identifies himself and specifically asks for Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Again, and finally, this particular journal, this again is contained in the journal which is dated 26 June, 1995 at its commencement and 24th July 1995 at its filing date, would you agree with me that this is another conversation that took place during those two dates, that you took down during those two dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 316C.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you look over that conversation and state whether or not you took that conversation down. It's a number of pages so look at every page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, to demonstrate the point, if you could just look at 316/1B, which is the final two pages of this document, it's the last two pages of this exhibit, and if you could look at that and then place it on the ELMO. Is that the typed copy of your conversation which you referred to earlier in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's the copy that would have been sent to the higher command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now, Mr. Usher, you could make available Prosecutor's Exhibit 294, and I'm afraid I can't give you a page number apart from 00782000. It's actually towards the end of this document. It's the sixth page from the end. 2000, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you look at the conversation, the bottom right-hand corner and over the next subsequent pages, and confirm that that is the intercept which I've just shown you. Look at all of the pages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has, in fact, confirmed that Prosecutor's Exhibit 316C is contained, beginning at page 00782000, in Prosecutor's Exhibit 294.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Witness -- the usher will need to help you here -- you could go back to page 00781988, do you see any date on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you leaf through those pages, between the page with the date on and the page where the intercept that you took down is found, and see if you find any other date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, just that one date, and this conversation was recorded on the same day, the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could, just for completeness, go to the end of that book, and could you state the date on which this book was finished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On what page is that date found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The one but last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not going to read this conversation; it's a very long one. I just will lay foundation for that with the witness. Mr. Usher, just so we can prepare ourselves, if you could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 283 at hand and also Prosecutor's Exhibit 317 and 318. We're nearly finished, Mr. Usher. This is a very short conversation. If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 317C.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could read that conversation over. You don't need to read it for the benefit of the Judges, I shall read it, but is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this a conversation which you wrote down? Is this an intercept which you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think again, if you look at the next page, there is another example of the report made to the higher command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 317/D. If that could be placed on the ELMO. Now, Witness, do you see a date on this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you read the date out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if you could turn to page 49 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 283. Your Honours, that is, in fact, page 00804843 in the evidence registration system, but there is a numbering system that was put there by the operators, and it's page 49 in the top right-hand corner, with the letters "WE" written underneath it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could look on that page and state whether or not you see the conversation which you've just identified to the Judges as being one of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has confirmed that the conversation in Exhibit 317 is contained in Prosecutor's Exhibit 283. If, Mr. Usher, you could turn back to page 46 of that diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, is there a date on this particular page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just go through the pages. Between the page with that date and the page on which is written the relevant conversation, do you see any other dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No. This conversation was on the same day, the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which, indeed, is the same date that's contained on the typewritten copy of the same conversation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to go to the end of this booklet, on the second to last page, if you could just -- I think it's a school child's geometry book that was used. What's the date that was written there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And is that the date when the book was closed or filed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes, when it was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will just read this conversation into the transcript, Mr. President. It has written at the top "785.000, Channel 5, at 1355 hours". "Participants: Colonel Milanovic - Palma (duty officer) M: Hello, Colonel Milanovic speaking. P: Go ahead, Colonel. M: Hey, listen, bud. Is your bulldozer somewhere around there, not the bulldozer but the one with the scoop, whatever you call it? P: Yes. M: Well, he should report to Konjevic Polje, to be there for us. P: ... M: And where on the ground is it, damn it? P: ... M: There is nothing before? P: No. M: Okay. Bye." And then it's signed --- there's a box indicating where the intercept was signed. Now, the last one that we're interested in, if that could be shown to the witness. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 318.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you recall, do you recall the call sign Palma, who that was within the VRS chain of command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: I think it was the Zvornik Brigade, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could look at 318/C, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And is this an intercept which you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could now turn finally, Mr. Usher, to Exhibit 283 and page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you see the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And is that the same conversation that you've just identified to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness has confirmed that the conversation contained in Prosecutor's Exhibit 318 is part of a notebook, Prosecutor's Exhibit 283 at page 00804845.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you could turn back to page 46, which is a page that we looked at previously, what is the date at the top of that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could go now through to the relevant conversation at page 50 of this booklet, and as you're going through, can you check if there are any other dates written in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: No, there aren't any. That was a conversation on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which day was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: The 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Actually, Mr. President, finally, I'll read this conversation into the record. The frequency is at the top, "785.000". "Channel 11, 1730 hours. Participants: X: Is it possible for us to send about ten buses from Bijeljina? Y: Well, tell them right away to come. There's about 6.000 of them now. X: Off military age? Y: Shut up, don't repeat. X: Okay. Then I'll send them? Y: Yeah, send them. I have three points, fuck it. There's the one where you and I were, then there's the one up there where the checkpoint at the intersection is, and there's the one halfway between the checkpoint and the loading place. X: So over there as well? Y: At each point there are roughly 1.500 to 2.000. X: And they're still transporting the women and children? Y: Well, there's still some left. X: I thought it was /finished/. We were there too, on the spot, there aren't that many of them. Y: Well, I was there just now. X: So there are still some? Y: Yeah, I just came /from there/. X: Okay. Then I have to send them and have them report there in Kasaba to the last. /as printed/ Y: Have them report to the stadium. X: Okay, we'll fill up over at Jovo's. Y: Let them fill up over there at Kundasevic's. X: Yeah, that's what I'm saying. Good. Y: Okay. Have them start right away. I'll see if I can get two more of those guys to drive. X: Give as many as you can. Over there I figured out not to use our Deutz /truck/. Y: Yeah, I know, I was with Radakovic. X: Because there's really no /need/. They can carry a small number, fuck it. There's no need and we might need them to transport units or something like that. Y: Yeah, I was with Radakovic. X: Is that job finished? Y: Well, they're at the intersection, gathering /them/. X: Good. Have 'em drive them away and then come back. Y: Well, they'll have to drive until they are all gone. X: Good. Okay, I'll tell him. Y: Okay, bye. X: Bye." And then there is a "/signed/".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you refer in this particular example to the participants as "X" and "Y". Is this an example of where, as you said earlier in your evidence, you couldn't identify the speakers in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS V
utterances.text: In every situation, there were occasions where they didn't introduce themselves and we were not able to put their names in, so we just say -- put an "X" or a "Y". Whenever they didn't actually introduce themselves, we would say "X" or "Y".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions for the witness, so I can offer him for cross-examination.
